voice.refText: You wake up and discover you can pause time. 10 seconds once a day. At first, you use it for dumb things. You catch your falling coffee. You dodge your boss in the hallway.

Lotte.describe: A low, warm female voice: a woman in her late fifties, a baker who has seen everything. Alto, slightly husky, unhurried and dry, a hint of a German accent. Speaks plainly, close to the listener.

Jonas.describe: A relaxed male baritone: a man of about thirty, the listener's flatmate. Young, warm and a little husky, quick and playful, easy laughter under the words, casual modern English.

Woman.describe: A sharp, bright female voice: a woman in her sixties on a city tram. Slightly nasal mezzo, quick and indignant, a voice that carries down the whole carriage.

Driver.describe: A flat, tired male baritone: a tram driver in his forties. Gravelly, bored and matter-of-fact, speaking over his shoulder like a public announcement.

Bank man.describe: A thin, precise male baritone: a bank officer in his fifties. Slightly nasal, polite and measured, every word chosen, a quiet clerk's restraint.

Flour man.describe: A deep, gravelly male bass: a delivery man in his forties who hauls flour sacks. Big, gruff, loud and blunt, a working man's voice from the back of a van.

lines.text: Lotte: You dropped your money.
lines.say: [amused, deadpan, looking down at the counter, a baker who has seen everything] You dropped your money.
lines.speaker: Lotte

lines.text: Jonas: That's the whole account?
lines.say: [dry disbelief, leaning in, half a laugh held back] That's the whole account?
lines.speaker: Jonas

lines.text: Lotte: One cent. You counted it, didn't you.
lines.say: [fond, mock-serious, holding the paper cent to the lamp like a jeweller] One cent. You counted it, didn't you.
lines.speaker: Lotte

lines.text: Jonas: You count everything.
lines.say: [affectionate, a shrug in the voice, said a hundred times before] You count everything.
lines.speaker: Jonas

lines.text: Lotte: In you go. Tomorrow, two.
lines.say: [playful, a nursery-rhyme promise, tapping the jar lid on the beats] In you go. Tomorrow, two.
lines.speaker: Lotte

lines.text: Jonas: Baker's magic?
lines.say: [teasing, eyebrows up, quick] Baker's magic?
lines.speaker: Jonas

lines.text: Lotte: Baker's maths. Counted?
lines.say: [brisk, business returning, palm already out, the question she asks everyone] Baker's maths. Counted?
lines.speaker: Lotte

lines.text: Jonas: Did your phone just... rip?
lines.say: [groggy, alarmed, whispered too loud, sitting up in the dark] Did your phone just... rip?
lines.speaker: Jonas

lines.text: Jonas: Two cents. Don't spend it all at once.
lines.say: [sleepy sarcasm, flat, the coat already going back over his head] Two cents. Don't spend it all at once.
lines.speaker: Jonas

lines.text: Two cents. Last night, one. You know that.
lines.say: [hushed, close to the mic, the first words of the narrator, a secret shared in the dark] Two cents. Last night, one. You know that.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: You always know the number.
lines.say: [warm, slow, a fact about a friend, a small smile] You always know the number.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: To the cent.
lines.say: [quiet, precise, the last word placed like a coin] To the cent.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: What if your money doubled every day?
lines.say: [curious, lifting, the question asked plainly to you, eyes wide] What if your money doubled every day?
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Every night. Whatever's there at midnight, twice by morning. From one cent. And it will not stop.
lines.say: [steady, building, each clause a step, the last four words cold and even] Every night. Whatever's there at midnight, twice by morning. From one cent. And it will not stop.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Here's the rule, once. At midnight, whatever's in your account doubles. New money. Taken from no one, the rule says.
lines.say: [clear, matter-of-fact, a teacher who likes you, a faint doubt on 'the rule says'] Here's the rule, once. At midnight, whatever's in your account doubles. New money. Taken from no one, the rule says.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: There is no off switch. Except one. Exactly zero at midnight. Not a cent more, not a cent less. Remember that.
lines.say: [lowered, deliberate, a finger raised, slowing on 'exactly zero', the last two words almost a warning] There is no off switch. Except one. Exactly zero at midnight. Not a cent more, not a cent less. Remember that.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Two cents. You laugh. So you do the sensible thing. Nothing. Jonas pays.
lines.say: [light, amused at you, a chuckle under 'nothing', the last two words a shrug] Two cents. You laugh. So you do the sensible thing. Nothing. Jonas pays.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Lotte doesn't laugh.
lines.say: [quiet, a small turn, the smile gone] Lotte doesn't laugh.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Lotte: My grandfather's story. The king's wheat.
lines.say: [low, tender, remembering, setting grains down one by one as she speaks] My grandfather's story. The king's wheat.
lines.speaker: Lotte

lines.text: A king, a chessboard. One grain on the first square, and double on every square after. By the last square, the board owes more wheat than the whole world grows in over a thousand years.
lines.say: [storytelling, hushed, patient at the start, a widening awe toward the end, no hype] A king, a chessboard. One grain on the first square, and double on every square after. By the last square, the board owes more wheat than the whole world grows in over a thousand years.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: But you're counting squares. The money's counting nights.
lines.say: [dry, cold, a turn of the head, the second sentence slower] But you're counting squares. The money's counting nights.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Day eleven. Ten euros. You've waited for this one.
lines.say: [bright, expectant, a little grin, the drum roll before a small moment] Day eleven. Ten euros. You've waited for this one.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Lotte: One forty. Counted?
lines.say: [brisk, unimpressed, palm out, exactly the same as every other morning] One forty. Counted?
lines.speaker: Lotte

lines.text: Jonas: Lotte. Lotte! Look who paid.
lines.say: [delighted, mock-astonished, tugging her sleeve, a stage whisper] Lotte. Lotte! Look who paid.
lines.speaker: Jonas

lines.text: Lotte: I saw.
lines.say: [flat, two words, writing on the board, not looking up] I saw.
lines.speaker: Lotte

lines.text: Jonas: Three years. Lottery?
lines.say: [teasing, warm, narrowing his eyes at you, a real question under the joke] Three years. Lottery?
lines.speaker: Jonas

lines.text: Day eighteen. Thirteen hundred euros. Jonas's birthday is Saturday. You order a cake.
lines.say: [cheerful, quick, a plan forming, pleased with yourself] Day eighteen. Thirteen hundred euros. Jonas's birthday is Saturday. You order a cake.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Day nineteen. Twenty-six hundred. You add a band.
lines.say: [giddy, a notch faster, the grin widening] Day nineteen. Twenty-six hundred. You add a band.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Day twenty-one. Ten thousand. You add the street, and you stop, because you've run out of street.
lines.say: [gleeful, almost laughing, tumbling forward, a comic stop on 'run out of street'] Day twenty-one. Ten thousand. You add the street, and you stop, because you've run out of street.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Jonas: Who are all these people?
lines.say: [bewildered, in pyjamas, blinking at the street, half asleep] Who are all these people?
lines.speaker: Jonas

lines.text: Lotte: Your party.
lines.say: [dry, arms folded behind a wall of cakes, exhausted and amused] Your party.
lines.speaker: Lotte

lines.text: Jonas: I said a small cake.
lines.say: [protesting, a little hurt, pointing at nothing] I said a small cake.
lines.speaker: Jonas

lines.text: Lotte: Your friend ordered thirty-one. Last night.
lines.say: [flat, a nod at you, the blame placed neatly] Your friend ordered thirty-one. Last night.
lines.speaker: Lotte

lines.text: Jonas: I'm thirty-one!
lines.say: [outraged and touched at once, loud, a laugh breaking through] I'm thirty-one!
lines.speaker: Jonas

lines.text: Lotte: Sixty-two cakes.
lines.say: [deadpan, wiping her hands] Sixty-two cakes.
lines.speaker: Lotte

lines.text: Jonas: Did you count the candles?
lines.say: [softening, a knife in a cake, a smile he tries to hide] Did you count the candles?
lines.speaker: Jonas

lines.text: Lotte: Counts everything, that one.
lines.say: [fond, quiet, the family joke handed back, almost tender] Counts everything, that one.
lines.speaker: Lotte

lines.text: Every morning you planned the party with that morning's number. Every morning the number had moved on without you. That's how a cake turns into a brass band.
lines.say: [amused, explaining, a wink in the voice, the last sentence landing like a punchline] Every morning you planned the party with that morning's number. Every morning the number had moved on without you. That's how a cake turns into a brass band.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Woman: Who's paying for all this?
lines.say: [suspicious, shopping bags in both hands, loud enough for the whole tram] Who's paying for all this?
lines.speaker: Woman

lines.text: Driver: The one in the scarf. Everyone rides free today.
lines.say: [bored, over the shoulder, a public announcement with no feeling in it] The one in the scarf. Everyone rides free today.
lines.speaker: Driver

lines.text: Woman: Why?
lines.say: [sharp, one word, genuinely baffled] Why?
lines.speaker: Woman

lines.text: Jonas: That one can't help it.
lines.say: [deadpan, from his seat, pretending not to know you, a sigh in it] That one can't help it.
lines.speaker: Jonas

lines.text: Woman: Well. I'm staying on, then.
lines.say: [decided, settling into her seat, bags on her lap, pleased with herself] Well. I'm staying on, then.
lines.speaker: Woman

lines.text: Thirty people ride to the end of the line and back. Because it's free. The whole tram, all day, costs less than tonight will hand you back before breakfast.
lines.say: [wry, fond of people, a chuckle on 'because it's free', the last clause a little dizzy] Thirty people ride to the end of the line and back. Because it's free. The whole tram, all day, costs less than tonight will hand you back before breakfast.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: But here's the problem. The party was a month's money. You thought. By the morning after, it was one night's worth.
lines.say: [uneasy, slowing, a cloud over the fun, 'you thought' set apart with a small wince] But here's the problem. The party was a month's money. You thought. By the morning after, it was one night's worth.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Ask people to carry on a doubling, and most guess far too low. You just did. In public. With a band.
lines.say: [embarrassed on your behalf, dry, the last three fragments each a small jab] Ask people to carry on a doubling, and most guess far too low. You just did. In public. With a band.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Each new night is worth more than every night before it, put together. So you weren't a little behind. You were living in the wrong week.
lines.say: [sober, careful, letting the arithmetic sink in, the last sentence quiet and a little frightening] Each new night is worth more than every night before it, put together. So you weren't a little behind. You were living in the wrong week.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: The number's ahead of you now. You can't catch it. But the bank can. It calls.
lines.say: [tense, low, a chase you are losing, the last two words clipped like a phone ringing] The number's ahead of you now. You can't catch it. But the bank can. It calls.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Bank man: Where does it come from?
lines.say: [polite, careful, pen poised, a man who already knows you will not have an answer] Where does it come from?
lines.speaker: Bank man

lines.text: Bank man: Mine. Right.
lines.say: [flat, repeating it back as he writes, not believing a word of it] Mine. Right.
lines.speaker: Bank man

lines.text: Bank man: If it's a mistake, we can take it back. All of it. In a few hours.
lines.say: [neutral, procedural, a door left open on purpose, 'all of it' slightly weighted] If it's a mistake, we can take it back. All of it. In a few hours.
lines.speaker: Bank man

lines.text: Bank man: Is it a mistake?
lines.say: [quiet, direct, looking at you over his glasses, a real question] Is it a mistake?
lines.speaker: Bank man

lines.text: He writes that down. You watch him write it. Remember that, too.
lines.say: [hushed, watchful, a plant laid gently, the last word an echo of the rule] He writes that down. You watch him write it. Remember that, too.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Day twenty-eight. One point three million. You buy the building. The bakery, the flats, the lot. Lotte never pays rent again.
lines.say: [warm, generous, proud of you, a breath of relief on the last sentence] Day twenty-eight. One point three million. You buy the building. The bakery, the flats, the lot. Lotte never pays rent again.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: You hand her the deed. She puts it under the till and slides you the same day-old roll. Free.
lines.say: [tender, amused, slowing on the roll, the last word soft] You hand her the deed. She puts it under the till and slides you the same day-old roll. Free.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Lotte: Day-old. Free.
lines.say: [gruff and kind, two words, no ceremony, the deed already forgotten] Day-old. Free.
lines.speaker: Lotte

lines.text: Day thirty-one. Lotte's counter.
lines.say: [plain, a date and a place, a breath held underneath] Day thirty-one. Lotte's counter.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Lotte: Morning. Counted?
lines.say: [cheerful, routine, palm out, chalk in the other hand] Morning. Counted?
lines.speaker: Lotte

lines.text: You hold the phone up to her. And the number won't fit.
lines.say: [quiet, then stopping short, a catch in the breath on 'won't fit'] You hold the phone up to her. And the number won't fit.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Ten million euros. Say it the other way. A billion. Cents.
lines.say: [awed, slow, each number weighed, a disbelieving half-laugh on 'cents'] Ten million euros. Say it the other way. A billion. Cents.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: For the first time in your life, you can't count it.
lines.say: [hushed, almost sad, the habit breaking, no music under it] For the first time in your life, you can't count it.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Jonas: Is that... all yours?
lines.say: [stunned, small, a loop of paper in his fingers, a joke he cannot find] Is that... all yours?
lines.speaker: Jonas

lines.text: And that's when you decide to get rid of it. The fun way.
lines.say: [mischievous, brightening, a door swinging open, 'the fun way' with a grin] And that's when you decide to get rid of it. The fun way.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: So you spend. Faster than it grows. Can you?
lines.say: [energised, a dare, quick, the question thrown to you] So you spend. Faster than it grows. Can you?
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Day thirty-three. Forty million euros. Jonas has a football club. Not supports. Has. The one at the end of the tram line, that loses every Saturday.
lines.say: [delighted, comic, the correction 'not supports, has' sharp and proud, fond on the losing] Day thirty-three. Forty million euros. Jonas has a football club. Not supports. Has. The one at the end of the tram line, that loses every Saturday.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Jonas: You bought my club.
lines.say: [dazed, flat, a statement he has to say out loud to believe] You bought my club.
lines.speaker: Jonas

lines.text: Jonas: They're winning.
lines.say: [alarmed, standing, as if reporting a fire] They're winning.
lines.speaker: Jonas

lines.text: Jonas: I don't know what to do with my hands when they win.
lines.say: [lost, comic, looking at his own hands, a man whose world has changed shape] I don't know what to do with my hands when they win.
lines.speaker: Jonas

lines.text: By Sunday you could have bought the league. Jonas only wanted the one that loses.
lines.say: [wry, then tender, the second sentence slower and a little sad] By Sunday you could have bought the league. Jonas only wanted the one that loses.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Day thirty-five. A hundred and seventy million. Lotte's rolls deserve the sky.
lines.say: [grand, mock-heroic, arms wide in the voice, enjoying the nonsense] Day thirty-five. A hundred and seventy million. Lotte's rolls deserve the sky.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Lotte: Where is it going?
lines.say: [flat, arms folded, squinting up at the balloon, not impressed] Where is it going?
lines.speaker: Lotte

lines.text: Jonas: Everywhere. Bread from the sky.
lines.say: [thrilled, holding a rope, a boy with a kite] Everywhere. Bread from the sky.
lines.speaker: Jonas

lines.text: Lotte: They'll be cold by the sky.
lines.say: [practical, dry, a baker's objection, no pause before it] They'll be cold by the sky.
lines.speaker: Lotte

lines.text: Jonas: People are ordering. Look. Forty.
lines.say: [excited, waving a phone at her, counting fast] People are ordering. Look. Forty.
lines.speaker: Jonas

lines.text: Lotte: I have two hands. I bake what I bake.
lines.say: [firm, calm, the line of the film said as a plain fact, turning to go inside] I have two hands. I bake what I bake.
lines.speaker: Lotte

lines.text: The balloon comes back with forty orders and no rolls.
lines.say: [deadpan, a beat of comic failure, the air going out of the joke] The balloon comes back with forty orders and no rolls.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Day thirty-seven. You stop reading the number before you spend. It makes no difference. Every morning, more than you started with.
lines.say: [tired, the fun gone flat, a treadmill in the voice, the last sentence heavy] Day thirty-seven. You stop reading the number before you spend. It makes no difference. Every morning, more than you started with.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Here's what you'd believed. Money is a pile of stuff. More money, more stuff.
lines.say: [gentle, patient, laying out the wrong idea without mockery] Here's what you'd believed. Money is a pile of stuff. More money, more stuff.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: It isn't. Money is a ticket for things people make. And Lotte bakes what Lotte bakes. Same rolls as last month. Your pile is a bigger ticket for the same bread.
lines.say: [clear, firm, the correction landing plainly, warmth on Lotte's name, the last sentence slow] It isn't. Money is a ticket for things people make. And Lotte bakes what Lotte bakes. Same rolls as last month. Your pile is a bigger ticket for the same bread.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: But everything you spend has to land somewhere. And it lands where you stand.
lines.say: [ominous, low, the second sentence quieter than the first, a door closing] But everything you spend has to land somewhere. And it lands where you stand.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Flour man: Triple.
lines.say: [blunt, one word, arms folded, no apology] Triple.
lines.speaker: Flour man

lines.text: Lotte: Triple? For flour?
lines.say: [shocked, rising, offended for her flour] Triple? For flour?
lines.speaker: Lotte

lines.text: Flour man: Everyone on this street spends the scarf's money now. I know who you're baking for.
lines.say: [hard, unhurried, a man who has done his sums, a nod toward your window on 'his'] Everyone on this street spends the scarf's money now. I know who you're baking for.
lines.speaker: Flour man

lines.text: Lotte: Same flour.
lines.say: [low, stubborn, two words through her teeth] Same flour.
lines.speaker: Lotte

lines.text: Flour man: Different street.
lines.say: [cold, final, lifting the sack off the van] Different street.
lines.speaker: Flour man

lines.text: Day forty. Your street's prices move first, because that's where you spend. One forty. Two ten. Three. Four twenty.
lines.say: [grim, even, each price a chalk stroke, no colour in the numbers] Day forty. Your street's prices move first, because that's where you spend. One forty. Two ten. Three. Four twenty.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Lotte: Same rolls.
lines.say: [quiet, bitter, to herself, wiping the board] Same rolls.
lines.speaker: Lotte

lines.text: Same rolls. Four twenty.
lines.say: [hollow, repeating her, the price said like an apology] Same rolls. Four twenty.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: She counts what her savings will buy. Last month, a year of flour. Tonight, four months. She didn't spend a cent.
lines.say: [hushed, aching, slow on 'half a year', the last sentence almost a whisper] She counts what her savings will buy. Last month, a year of flour. Tonight, four months. She didn't spend a cent.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Lotte: A third.
lines.say: [barely voiced, one word, the pencil stopped, looking up at the framed note] A third.
lines.speaker: Lotte

lines.text: So she knows what you haven't said.
lines.say: [guilty, low, close, the admission coming] So she knows what you haven't said.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: It isn't taken from anyone. Except it is. From everyone. A little. Every night.
lines.say: [the turn: quiet, confessional, each fragment heavier, 'every night' almost broken] It isn't taken from anyone. Except it is. From everyone. A little. Every night.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: You counted the price of a roll to the cent for years. Now it won't fit on the board.
lines.say: [sad, plain, the habit from the first minute coming back wounded] You counted the price of a roll to the cent for years. Now it won't fit on the board.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: So you try the obvious thing. You give it away. Day forty-five, a year's rent for everyone on the street. Lotte's flour, paid from your account every morning, from now on.
lines.say: [hopeful, hurrying, a fix being tried, warmth on the flour] So you try the obvious thing. You give it away. Day forty-five, a year's rent for everyone on the street. Lotte's flour, paid from your account every morning, from now on.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Lotte: Flour. Not money.
lines.say: [firm, kind, pushing the envelope back, a rule of her own] Flour. Not money.
lines.speaker: Lotte

lines.text: By Saturday the board moves again. Six thirty. Because every envelope was new money. Chasing the same rolls.
lines.say: [deflating, the hope going out, the explanation patient and sorry] By Saturday the board moves again. Six thirty. Because every envelope was new money. Chasing the same rolls.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Mansa Musa's gifts kept gold cheap in Cairo for at least twelve years. Your gifts do it to bread. Ask Jonas.
lines.say: [storytelling, a little wonder, then dry and quick on the second sentence] Mansa Musa's gifts kept gold cheap in Cairo for at least twelve years. Your gifts do it to bread. Ask Jonas.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Jonas: Six thirty? Since when?
lines.say: [thrown, counting coins, a laugh that does not come] Six thirty? Since when?
lines.speaker: Jonas

lines.text: Lotte: Since that one.
lines.say: [quiet, not unkind, a nod at you, the truth said once] Since that one.
lines.speaker: Lotte

lines.text: Jonas: Not me.
lines.say: [gentle, immovable, two words, shaking his head at the phone] Not me.
lines.speaker: Jonas

lines.text: Jonas: Then it's me making the rolls cost that. I'd rather owe you one.
lines.say: [soft, steady, a man explaining himself for once, a small smile at the end] Then it's me making the rolls cost that. I'd rather owe you one.
lines.speaker: Jonas

lines.text: Three problems. One, you can't spend it. Two, you can't give it. Three, you can't hand it over. Whoever holds it makes the bread cost more.
lines.say: [clipped, counting on fingers, the trap closing, the last sentence slower] Three problems. One, you can't spend it. Two, you can't give it. Three, you can't hand it over. Whoever holds it makes the bread cost more.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: And the only exit is the number you were told to remember on day two.
lines.say: [low, a thread pulled tight, the plant coming back, almost a whisper on 'day two'] And the only exit is the number you were told to remember on day two.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Day fifty-five. The number passes what the whole world makes in a year. Every loaf, every car, every hour of work on Earth. About 128 trillion dollars.
lines.say: [awed and afraid, slow, the list building, the figure said plainly, no hype] Day fifty-five. The number passes what the whole world makes in a year. Every loaf, every car, every hour of work on Earth. About a hundred and twenty-eight trillion dollars.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: You have more than that. Above a bakery. And tomorrow is twice this.
lines.say: [hushed, absurd and terrible, a dry breath on 'above a bakery', the last sentence cold] You have more than that. Above a bakery. And tomorrow is twice this.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Here's your choice. Erase it now, and Lotte loses tomorrow's flour, the one promise you kept. Wait one night to keep it, and the street takes one more doubling.
lines.say: [tense, even, both sides given equal weight, a real dilemma put to you, no lean] Here's your choice. Erase it now, and Lotte loses tomorrow's flour, the one promise you kept. Wait one night to keep it, and the street takes one more doubling.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: You call the man from the bank. Now.
lines.say: [decided, fast, a breath before 'now', the figure already moving] You call the man from the bank. Now.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Bank man: So it was a mistake.
lines.say: [quiet, on speaker, a statement and a question, no triumph in it] So it was a mistake.
lines.speaker: Bank man

lines.text: Bank man: Everything goes. Your wages too. You understand?
lines.say: [careful, slower, a man making sure, a touch of pity on 'your wages too'] Everything goes. Your wages too. You understand?
lines.speaker: Bank man

lines.text: Bank man: Fifty minutes.
lines.say: [brisk, procedural, the keyboard already going] Fifty minutes.
lines.speaker: Bank man

lines.text: Zero. Everything. Your wages, your savings, three years of roll money. Ten minutes to midnight. You breathe out.
lines.say: [drained, relieved, the list quiet and even, a real exhale on the last three words] Zero. Everything. Your wages, your savings, three years of roll money. Ten minutes to midnight. You breathe out.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Then the phone buzzes. A refund. From the tram app. From the day you paid for the whole tram. One cent.
lines.say: [alarmed, sharp, the fun of the tram turned to dread, 'one cent' small and terrible] Then the phone buzzes. A refund. From the tram app. From the day you paid for the whole tram. One cent.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: One cent at midnight is two. Two is four. And it all starts again. Three minutes.
lines.say: [panicked, fast, the doubling heard as a clock, the last two words urgent] One cent at midnight is two. Two is four. And it all starts again. Three minutes.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Who do you pay a cent to, at three minutes to midnight?
lines.say: [breathless, a question to you and to yourself, already running down the stairs] Who do you pay a cent to, at three minutes to midnight?
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Lotte: Counted?
lines.say: [tired, warm, through a door opened a hand's width, the gag one last time, almost a kindness] Counted?
lines.speaker: Lotte

lines.text: You count. One cent. Into her palm. For every day-old roll she never charged you for. She closes her hand.
lines.say: [tender, very slow, close, each fragment placed like the coin, the last sentence barely spoken] You count. One cent. Into her palm. For every day-old roll she never charged you for. She closes her hand.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Zero, doubled, is zero.
lines.say: [quiet, complete, after the silence, a thing finally true, no music] Zero, doubled, is zero.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Day fifty-six. Jonas pays. He always pays.
lines.say: [morning, plain, a small smile, back where we began] Day fifty-six. Jonas pays. He always pays.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: You know the number.
lines.say: [warm, soft, the first minute's line returned and meaning something else] You know the number.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: The board says three ninety. Down a little. Not back. It won't come back.
lines.say: [honest, unsentimental, a cost admitted, the last sentence gentle but firm] The board says three ninety. Down a little. Not back. It won't come back.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: Lotte slides you the day-old roll. In her other hand, last night's cent. She hasn't put it in the till.
lines.say: [tender, hushed, noticing, slowing on the cent] Lotte slides you the day-old roll. In her other hand, last night's cent. She hasn't put it in the till.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: A coin isn't a thing. It's Lotte, agreeing to bake tomorrow.
lines.say: [quiet, clear, the one idea to take home, said as a complete thought, warmth on her name] A coin isn't a thing. It's Lotte, agreeing to bake tomorrow.
lines.speaker: narrator

lines.text: So, would you have erased it? Tell us in the comments. And if you'd have done the same, hit like and subscribe.
lines.say: [direct, friendly, lighter, the question real and the invitation easy, no hype] So, would you have erased it? Tell us in the comments. And if you'd have done the same, hit like and subscribe.
lines.speaker: narrator
